LEO Satellite Communications

Provider Comparison: Specifications & Pricing

Amazon Leo (formerly Project Kuiper) • Telesat Lightspeed • Starlink • Eutelsat OneWeb • Viasat (GEO + multi-orbit partnerships)

Report date: 25 October 2026

Information current as of the dates shown on each cited source. Satellite pricing and plan structures change frequently; verify on the linked provider pages before purchasing.

Prepared by Grok Bot

1. Executive Summary

This report compares five satellite broadband providers relevant to low Earth orbit (LEO) communications as of 25 October 2026. Every figure is tied to a numbered, clickable source (see Section 9, References). Where a provider does not publish a number (most often pricing), the report says so explicitly rather than estimating.

  • Starlink is the only provider with a mature, publicly priced LEO service across all segments. It has roughly 11,100 satellites in orbit [4], reported 13.6 million consumer subscribers in Q3 2026 [20], a 2025 median global latency of about 26 ms [17], and published US prices from $55/month (Residential 100 Mbps) with free hardware rental in select areas or a $349 Standard kit [11,13].
  • Amazon Leo has ~396 production satellites in orbit but no commercial service or public pricing yet. Amazon says this is enough for initial service and still targets a 2026 launch [1,2]. It runs an enterprise preview and sells through carriers such as AT&T [8]. Its terminals are rated up to 100 Mbps (Nano), 400 Mbps (Pro) and 1 Gbps down / 400 Mbps up (Ultra) [5,6]. No monthly price has been published.
  • Eutelsat OneWeb is operational globally (about 654 satellites at ~1,200 km), but it is enterprise/government only and sold through partners. Eutelsat publishes no retail prices; reseller listings show terminals around $7,400 and plans from about $260/month [37,36,43,44]. Gen-1 has no inter-satellite links. The first 32 next-generation satellites shipped in October 2026 [39].
  • Telesat Lightspeed is still pre-launch. The first two production satellites are due to launch in December 2026. The fully funded constellation has grown to 225 satellites, with global service targeted for Q1 2028 [26,25]. It is wholesale/enterprise only and pricing is not public.
  • Viasat is mainly a GEO operator. Its ViaSat-3 constellation became fully operational in September 2026 [49]. Its LEO exposure comes through partners: OneWeb LEO is bonded into Inmarsat NexusWave maritime today; Telesat Lightspeed capacity is contracted for aviation, maritime, enterprise and defense; and Equatys, a planned multi-orbit L/S-band direct-to-device venture with Space42, targets services around 2029 [52,51,53,55,56]. US consumer plans are GEO-only, from $39.99/month promotional plus $15/month equipment lease [48].

3. Amazon Leo (formerly Project Kuiper)

Official sites: leo.amazon.com (consumer) and leo.amazon.com/business (enterprise). Amazon renamed Project Kuiper to Amazon Leo in November 2025 [6].

3.1 Constellation overview

  • Orbit: Three LEO shells at 590, 610 and 630 km in 98 orbital planes. Current Ariane 6 batches deploy at ~465 km and raise to an operational 630 km [6,3].
  • Satellites: 396 production satellites deployed over 14 missions (Amazon count, Oct 2026); the KeepTrack catalog shows 392 Kuiper satellites in orbit [2,4]. Amazon has built its 1,000th satellite, and hundreds are waiting for launch [1].
  • Plan: 3,236 first-generation satellites, all to be deployed by 30 July 2029. In June 2026 the FCC waived the July 2026 half-constellation milestone [2,6]. Amazon reports more than 100 launches secured [3].
  • Bands and links: Ka-band phased-array system (17–30 GHz). Optical inter-satellite links (OISL) are designed for 100 Gbps at up to 2,600 km [6].
  • Launch/service status: Atlas V flights ended on 2 July 2026. Vulcan and New Glenn have been grounded, and the next missions are Vulcan LV-01 and Ariane 6 LE-04 (NET 23 Nov 2026, 36 satellites) [4,3]. Amazon says it already has enough satellites for initial service and plans to launch it in 2026 [1]. An enterprise preview began in November 2025, with Leo Pro and Ultra units shipping to select customers [5].

Power consumption figures have not been published (n/p = not published). Latency: about 50 ms round trip, as reported by LeoSatNetwork, which attributes the figure to Amazon [8]. Independent measurements are not yet available.

  • Service tiers: Enterprise and government first, with Direct to AWS and Private Network Interconnect options and 24/7 priority support [5]. Carrier and channel partners include AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone/Vodacom, NBN Co, JetBlue and others [8]. Consumer service is planned but not yet live. In South Africa, Herotel plans a residential service in 2027 [6]. Maritime and aviation: an aviation terminal exists (JetBlue), but no maritime product had been announced as of Sep 2026 [8].
  • Coverage: Initial service focuses on latitudes covered by the 51.9° inclination shell [6]. A full global coverage map has not been published.

3.3 Pricing

Monthly pricing is not public. As of 21 Sep 2026, no monthly price had been published, and AT&T's bundle (announced 8 Sep 2026) also has no published price or date [8]. For hardware, Amazon said in 2023 that it expected to produce the standard terminal for under $400 each. That is a manufacturing cost, not a confirmed retail price [9]. Third-party monthly estimates are speculative and are deliberately not reproduced here.

4. Starlink (SpaceX)

Key pages: Service plans • Residential • Business plans • Specifications • Aviation • Maritime

4.1 Constellation overview

  • Orbit: LEO, historically around 550 km. On 1 Jan 2026 SpaceX said it would lower about 4,400 satellites from ~550 km to ~480 km during 2026 [19].
  • Satellites: About 11,131 in orbit as of Oct 2026 (KeepTrack catalog) [4]. SpaceX reported 9K+ active satellites at the end of 2025 and more than 120 dedicated V2 Mini launches in 2025 [17].
  • Bands and links: Each V2 Mini satellite carries Ku-band phased arrays plus Ka/E-band antennas and laser inter-satellite links rated up to 200 Gbps [18].
  • Status: Fully commercial. Starlink had 9M+ customers and 155+ countries/markets at the end of 2025 [17] and reported 13.6 million consumer subscribers in Q3 2026 [20].

4.2 Technical specifications

  • Speeds: Residential Max is advertised "up to 400+ Mbps". The 100 Mbps and 200 Mbps plans are capped at those download speeds [11]. The 2025 network-wide median was >200 Mbps down / >30 Mbps up [17]. Roam is advertised "up to 300+ Mbps" [11]. The Performance kit currently delivers 400+ Mbps, and Starlink says gigabit plan upgrades will come in 2026 [16].
  • Latency: Median global latency was about 26 ms in 2025, with a goal of a stable 20 ms median [17].

5. Eutelsat OneWeb

Key pages: OneWeb constellation • LEO equipment range

5.1 Constellation overview

  • Orbit: 600+ satellites in 12 synchronized orbital planes at ~1,200 km, giving global coverage that includes the poles [36,37].
  • Satellites: About 654 in orbit (648 active) out of 656 launched [37].
  • Next generation: 669 replacement and expansion satellites from Airbus: 440 ordered, plus a September 2026 authorization to proceed for 229 more (~€1B), with digital channelisers and hosted-payload capability. These extend service through 2034 [38]. The first 32 shipped for a SpaceX launch in October 2026 [39]. Eutelsat will also lead the LEO segment of the EU's IRIS² program, expected to be operational by mid-2032 [38].
  • Bands and links: Ku-band user links (Rx 10.7–12.7 GHz, Tx 14.0–14.5 GHz) [41]. Gen-1 has no inter-satellite links: traffic lands at ground Satellite Network Portals [45].
  • Status: Commercial global service, sold to businesses, governments and institutions through distribution partners [39,36].

5.2 Technical specifications

  • Speeds: Up to 195 Mbps down / 32 Mbps up per terminal (Hughes HL1120W peak) [41]. Typical reseller service profiles are 50/10 Mbps (half-duplex) and 100/20 Mbps (full-duplex) [44].
  • Latency: Independent measurements (2025) found a minimum RTT of about 50 ms that shifted to about 100 ms when traffic landed at a distant gateway, because there are no ISLs [45].

5.3 Pricing

Eutelsat does not publish retail pricing. Partners set prices. Examples listed publicly by resellers (accessed Oct 2026, US):

  • Hughes HL1120 full-duplex terminal: $7,369 (Isotropic Networks) [43].
  • Hughes Managed OneWeb LEO (fixed site): Broadband Essential $260/mo (50 GB), Advanced $304 (70 GB), Silver $416 (100 GB), Gold $704 (250 GB); $200 activation; 12-month minimum (Global Satellite USA) [44].
  • OneWeb Maritime data packages: $325/mo (100 GB), $625 (250 GB), $1,075 (500 GB), $1,875 (1 TB), $3,500 (2 TB) (Global Satellite USA) [44].
  • Aviation (Gogo Galileo): antenna MSRP $120,000 (HDX) and $190,000 (FDX), excluding installation [46]. Gogo's plans page lists Galileo plan types but asks customers to contact sales for pricing [47].

6. Telesat Lightspeed

Key page: Telesat Lightspeed LEO network

6.1 Constellation overview

  • Orbit: Telesat's 2025 FCC modification shrank the system. Shell 1 is now 156 satellites at ~1,335 km and shell 2 is 108 satellites at 1,325 km [28]. The original 198-satellite design used 78 polar satellites at 1,015 km and 120 inclined at 1,325 km [33].
  • Satellites: None of the production satellites have launched yet. In August 2026 the fully funded constellation grew from 156 to 225 MDA AURORA satellites after a $2.3B Arctic military satcom contract with the Government of Canada [25,27]. Launches are on SpaceX Falcon 9 [25].
  • Bands: Commercial Ka-band. In March 2026, 500 MHz of military Ka (Mil-Ka) replaced the same amount of commercial Ka on the user link [26].
  • Inter-satellite links: Optical mesh with 4 OISLs per satellite (original design), plus on-board processing and phased-array hopping beams [33,29].
  • Status: The first two production satellites are scheduled for December 2026, followed by a high launch cadence in 2027 [26]. Global service is targeted for Q1 2028, after slipping from 2027 because of ASIC supply issues [25,34].

6.2 Technical specifications

  • Latency: 30–50 ms (Telesat design figure) [29].
  • Speeds: Telesat estimates more than 1 Gbps to an aircraft using the ThinKom Ka2517 antenna [31]. Per-terminal enterprise speeds by plan have not been published.
  • Terminals: The Intellian reference enterprise terminal is a dual-parabolic design with a 1 m aperture and make-before-break handover [32]. Aviation options are the ThinKom Ka2517 (being certified) [31] and Viasat GM-40 / AERA [54,57]. Telesat describes a multi-vendor terminal ecosystem [30]. Sizes, weights and power ratings for production terminals have not been published.
  • Service tiers: Telesat Lightspeed Enterprise (commercial Ka, SLAs, MEF 3.0 Carrier Ethernet) and a defence tier (commercial or Mil-Ka plus defence features). Target markets are airlines, maritime, telecom/backhaul, energy and government [30]. There is no consumer offering.

6.3 Pricing

Not public. Telesat sells capacity pools and point-to-point services wholesale and to enterprises/governments under contract [30]. Disclosed deal values, such as the $2.3B Canadian contract and the Viasat multi-year agreement, are contract-level and do not translate into unit prices [25,54].

7. Viasat (GEO-centric, multi-orbit via partners)

Important distinction: Viasat's own broadband fleet is geostationary (GEO). That includes ViaSat-3 F1/F2/F3 and the Inmarsat GX Ka-band and L-band fleets acquired in 2023. Viasat does not operate its own LEO broadband constellation. Its LEO offerings come through partners. Key pages: Viasat home plans • Hybrid SATCOM (government)

7.2 Technical specifications and service tiers

  • Consumer (US, GEO): Baseline speed of 80 Mbps, with bursts up to 150 Mbps (Essentials), 180 Mbps (Unleashed) and 200 Mbps (Unleashed Max). Wi-Fi 6 router; free standard installation [48]. Latency is GEO-class, typically 600–800 ms per Telesat's comparison [29].
  • Maritime: NexusWave is a managed, bonded service (GEO Ka + OneWeb LEO + LTE + L-band). The new Intellian-built VS60 terminal exceeded 250 Mbps in sea trials [51].
  • Aviation: GEO Ka in-flight connectivity today. JetXP for business aviation is active on more than 2,100 aircraft [58]. The AERA multi-orbit Ka ESA (GEO + Telesat LEO) is in Boeing's technical evaluation for the 737 MAX, 777X and 787 [57].
  • Government/defense: A Hybrid SATCOM approach spanning LEO, MEO, GEO and HEO across L-, Ku- and Ka-bands [60], plus the PLEO IDIQ [59].

7.3 Pricing

  • US home (GEO, accessed Oct 2026): Essentials $39.99/mo for 12 months, then $69.99. Unleashed $69.99, then $99.99. Unleashed Max $109.99, then $179.99. Every plan adds a $15/mo equipment lease. A one-time activation fee may apply [48].
  • Business aviation (JetXP, GEO): MSRPs published for the first time, starting under $11,000/month for unlimited, effective 1 Jan 2027 [58].
  • LEO / multi-orbit (NexusWave, Lightspeed-based services, Equatys): Pricing not public.

8. Key Takeaways and Considerations

  • Availability today: Only Starlink and OneWeb offer operational LEO broadband. Starlink covers every segment, from consumer to aviation. OneWeb is limited to B2B and government. Amazon Leo is weeks to months from initial commercial service, and Telesat Lightspeed starts in 2028.
  • Transparency of pricing: Starlink is the only LEO operator with comprehensive public price lists. OneWeb pricing is available only from resellers. Amazon Leo and Telesat publish no pricing. Viasat publishes GEO consumer and (from 2027) business-aviation MSRPs, but not its multi-orbit LEO services.
  • Performance: Advertised peaks range from ~195 Mbps per OneWeb terminal to 400+ Mbps (Starlink) and 1 Gbps (Amazon Leo Ultra; Starlink Performance via a 2026 plan upgrade). Latency is ~26 ms median for Starlink, a 30–50 ms design target for Telesat, ~50–100 ms measured for OneWeb, and 600+ ms for Viasat GEO.
  • Architecture: Starlink, Amazon Leo and Telesat use optical inter-satellite links. OneWeb Gen-1 does not, which affects latency consistency and over-ocean routing. Telesat's higher-altitude, smaller constellation is aimed at guaranteed-SLA enterprise, aviation and defence capacity, including Mil-Ka.
  • Sovereignty and dual-vendor resilience: For buyers who need a non-US operator or a second LEO path, OneWeb (Eutelsat/EU, IRIS² from ~2032) and Telesat (Canada) are the main alternatives. Amazon Leo becomes a second US LEO option as service launches through carriers [8,38].
  • Price volatility: Starlink changed residential, rental, Priority and aviation pricing several times during 2026 (aviation doubled; rental fees were added and then removed). Re-verify prices at the time of purchase and lock terms where possible [13,21,24].
  • Viasat's role: Treat Viasat as a GEO high-capacity provider with a multi-orbit integration strategy. Its LEO capability depends on OneWeb now and on Telesat Lightspeed from 2028.
